glossary.definition: Three seafaring peoples from northern Germany and Denmark who rowed across the North Sea to settle Britain after AD 410.
The Old English word for a warrior king who protected his kingdom and rewarded loyal fighters in his mead hall.
An ordinary free Anglo-Saxon farmer who ploughed fields, kept livestock, wove wool, and owed service to his lord.
Woven hazel sticks plastered with sticky mud, clay, and straw to build warm walls inside timber village homes.
A grand rectangular timber building with a central hearth fire where an Anglo-Saxon ruler feasted and held council.
Historians' name for the seven main Anglo-Saxon kingdoms: Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, and Wessex.
Royal burial mounds in Suffolk where archaeologists in 1939 uncovered an Anglo-Saxon ship imprint and helmet from around AD 625.
Precious weapons, jewellery, coins, and feasting vessels buried beside an important person to show status or for the afterlife.
A religious messenger, such as Augustine or Aidan, sent to a new land to preach and persuade people to become Christians.
A community where Christian monks or nuns lived to pray, farm, study, and copy sacred books by hand.
Smooth, strong writing sheets scraped and stretched from calfskin for monks to paint illuminated Gospel books with feather quills.
Straight-lined letters from the early Germanic and Norse alphabet, carved onto wood, metal, and tall outdoor stone crosses.
The northern European homelands of the Vikings, made up of modern Norway, Denmark, and Sweden.
The Viking shipbuilding method of overlapping split oak planks held with iron rivets and sealed watertight with tarred wool.
Needing barely one metre of water depth to float, letting Viking longships beach on sand and row far up rivers.
The huge Viking invasion force that landed in AD 865 under Ivar the Boneless, Halfdan, and Guthrum to conquer land.
An Anglo-Saxon part-time army of local free farmers and warriors called together by their king whenever invaders attacked.
A tight battle line where warriors stood shoulder to shoulder locking round wooden shields together like an unbroken fence.
The large area of northern and eastern England settled and ruled under Danish laws after Alfred's peace treaty in AD 878.
A fortified Anglo-Saxon town ringed with high earth ramparts, ditches, and timber gates, giving us our modern word borough.
The bustling Viking craft centre and river trading port captured in AD 866, lying beneath the streets of modern York.
A pure silver coin minted in Islamic cities such as Baghdad and Samarkand, traded along rivers by Viking merchants.
A wide, deep-hulled wooden Viking cargo ship built to carry settler families, livestock, and trade goods across open oceans.
An outdoor Viking community law-assembly where free men and women gathered to vote on laws and settle arguments fairly.
King Alfred's bold daughter, the Lady of the Mercians, who built walled burhs and led armies to recapture Viking Derby and Leicester.
Meaning Dane-gold, huge sums of silver pennies taxed from English families to pay raiding Viking fleets to sail away.
The royal council of wise Anglo-Saxon bishops and powerful earls who advised the king and chose the next monarch.
An elite full-time royal bodyguard warrior armed with a heavy two-handed battle-axe who protected kings such as Cnut and Harold Godwinson.

eras.headline: Guthrum's Midwinter Strike Forces Alfred Into the Marshes
eras.summary: After conquering York, East Anglia, and Mercia, Guthrum seized Chippenham in January AD 878 and drove King Alfred into hiding at Athelney in the Somerset marshes.

pillars.status: Holds northern and eastern England plus Chippenham in Wessex
Small loyal band planning a spring fightback on Athelney

eras.year: May AD 878 Battle of Edington and Danelaw Treaty
eras.headline: Shield Wall Victory at Edington Splits England Along Watling Street
eras.summary: Alfred rallied the Wessex fyrd at Egbert's Stone and defeated Guthrum at Edington. Guthrum was baptised as Aethelstan, and their treaty divided England into Saxon lands and the Danelaw.

pillars.status: Governs northern and eastern Danelaw farms under Danish law
Rules Wessex, western Mercia, and walled London from AD 886

eras.headline: 33 Fortified Burhs, 60-Oar Warships, and Schools of Learning
eras.summary: Alfred ringed Wessex with 33 earth-walled burhs no further than 20 miles apart, launched fast 60-oar coastal warships, and opened court schools translating Latin into Old English.

pillars.status: Checked by walled burh garrisons and coastal patrol ships
33 fortified burhs, royal fleet, and strong Saxon kingdom

source_texts.text: Artefact note: Photographed from both sides above a millimetre scale, this crescent-shaped bronze brooch fragment shows a smooth curved back on the left. On the right, bright gold coating gleams across a beaded rim, a raised four-sided frame, and deep spiral grooves.

Artefact note: Blown from thin olive-green and amber glass, this tall drinking vessel has fine horizontal glass threads wrapped around its flared rim. Two rows of dark hollow glass claws curve down the sides toward a tiny, narrow foot at the base.

Artefact note: Shining silvered panels stamped with warrior scenes and braided knotwork cover the dome and hinged cheek-guards of this full-face helmet. Tiny square red garnets line two arched golden eyebrows beside a gilded nose-guard and engraved moustache plate.

Artefact note: Rising over four metres tall beside a Cumbria stone church and smaller gravestones, this weathered sandstone shaft stands outdoors in all weathers. Three deep arched niches hold carved robed figures separated by rectangular panels of straight-lined Old English runes.

Artefact note: Carved in deep relief across a round-topped pale sandstone slab, seven marching figures stride forward in a tight single line. Each figure wears a ridged knee-length tunic and raises heavy weapons high above a smooth, rounded head.

Artefact note: Seen in close-up, this polished Viking sword hilt features a five-lobed metal pommel split into neat sections by braided silver wire. Below it, coiled copper-red animal patterns gleam along the curved guard above a wire-wrapped grip.

Artefact note: Lined up in a row beside black-and-white centimetre scale bars, these four rounded gaming counters each measure barely two centimetres across. Their smooth, dome-shaped tops still carry mottled brown soil marks from centuries buried underground.

Artefact note: In a grassy Cumbria churchyard, this slender red sandstone shaft towers over twice as tall as the visitor beside it. Above a smooth round base, braided stone carvings and figure panels rise to a wheel-ringed cross head.
